title: CUET Physics Test 3
subject: Physics (Code: 322)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Physics - 322.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Physics papers 2024, 2025 and 2026, analysed for format and level (no questions copied)

instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
Calculators are not allowed; numbers are chosen so the working can be done by hand.

questions.sub_topic: Energies of the hydrogen atom
questions.question:
Match each quantity for the hydrogen atom in List-I with its value in List-II.

List-I
(A) Energy of the ground state
(B) Energy needed to ionise the atom from \(n = 2\)
(C) First excitation energy
(D) Energy of the photon emitted in the jump \(n = 3 \to n = 1\)

List-II
(I) 12.09 eV
(II) 10.2 eV
(III) \(-13.6\) eV
(IV) 3.4 eV
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Step 1: \(E_1 = -13.6\) eV (III)
Step 2: From \(n = 2\): \(0 - (-3.4) = 3.4\) eV (IV)
Step 3: \(n = 1 \to 2\): \(-3.4 - (-13.6) = 10.2\) eV (II)
Step 4: \(n = 3 \to 1\): \(-1.51 - (-13.6) = 12.09\) eV (I)
Common mistake: Swapping (B) and (C); ionising from \(n = 2\) needs only 3.4 eV, while exciting from \(n = 1\) to 2 needs 10.2 eV.
Key point: Every energy here is a difference of \(E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}\) eV.

questions.sub_topic: Resistivity from a wire's resistance and size
questions.question: A wire 2 m long with a cross-section of 1 mm² has a resistance of \(4\ \Omega\). The resistivity of its material is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(2 \times 10^{-6}\ \Omega\) m
Given: \(l = 2\) m, \(A = 10^{-6}\) m², \(R = 4\ \Omega\)
Formula: \(\rho = \dfrac{RA}{l}\)
Step 1: \(\rho = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{2} = 2 \times 10^{-6}\ \Omega\) m
Common mistake: \(2 \times 10^{-4}\) (B) takes 1 mm² as \(10^{-4}\) m². \(8 \times 10^6\) (C) uses \(\dfrac{Rl}{A}\).
Key point: Resistivity is resistance scaled to unit length and unit area.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Formulas of photon and matter-wave quantities
questions.question:
Match each quantity in List-I with its expression in List-II.

List-I
(A) Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons
(B) Momentum of a photon
(C) de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through \(V\)
(D) Energy of a photon of wavelength \(\lambda\)

List-II
(I) \(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\)
(II) \(\dfrac{h}{\lambda}\)
(III) \(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}\)
(IV) \(h\nu - \phi_0\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Step 1: Einstein's equation: \(K_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0\) (IV)
Step 2: \(p = \dfrac{E}{c} = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}\) (II)
Step 3: \(p = \sqrt{2meV}\), so \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}\) (III)
Step 4: \(E = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\) (I)
Common mistake: Swapping (B) and (D); momentum has no \(c\), energy has.
Key point: For a photon, \(E = pc\).

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Motion of a diamagnetic sample in a non-uniform field
questions.question: A diamagnetic substance placed in a non-uniform magnetic field tends to move:
options: A) towards the stronger part of the field
B) round in a circle about the field
C) from the stronger to the weaker part
D) along the field without moving across it
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) from the stronger to the weaker part
Why: A diamagnetic substance is magnetised opposite to the applied field, so it is repelled from regions of strong field.
Why not the others: (A) describes paramagnetic and ferromagnetic substances. (B) and (D) have no basis.
Key point: Diamagnets are pushed out of strong fields; a superconductor is the extreme case.

questions.sub_topic: Meaning of coherent sources
questions.question: Two sources of light are coherent when they:
options: A) have a constant phase difference
D) are placed very close to each other
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) have a constant phase difference
Why: A steady interference pattern needs the phase difference between the waves to stay fixed in time.
Why not the others: Equal amplitudes or intensities (B, C) give dark fringes of zero intensity but do not make sources coherent. Closeness (D) affects the fringe width, not coherence.
Key point: Two separate bulbs are never coherent; YDSE splits light from one source.

questions.sub_topic: Wires of one material in increasing order of resistance
questions.question:
Four wires are made of the same material. Arrange them in increasing order of resistance:
(A) length \(l\), cross-section \(A\)
(B) length \(2l\), cross-section \(A\)
(C) length \(l\), cross-section \(2A\)
(D) length \(2l\), cross-section \(\dfrac{A}{2}\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (C), (A), (B), (D)
Step 1: \(R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A}\); call \(\dfrac{\rho l}{A} = R_0\)
Step 2: (A) \(R_0\); (B) \(2R_0\); (C) \(\dfrac{R_0}{2}\); (D) \(4R_0\)
Step 3: Increasing: (C), (A), (B), (D)
Common mistake: (D) reverses the order by taking \(R \propto A\).
Key point: Resistance rises with length and falls with cross-section.

questions.sub_topic: Wavelength emitted in the n = 2 to n = 1 jump
questions.question: The wavelength of the photon emitted when a hydrogen electron falls from \(n = 2\) to \(n = 1\) is about (\(hc = 1240\) eV nm):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 122 nm
Given: \(E_2 = -3.4\) eV, \(E_1 = -13.6\) eV
Formula: \(\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E_2 - E_1}\)
Step 1: \(E_2 - E_1 = 10.2\) eV
Step 2: \(\lambda = \dfrac{1240}{10.2} \approx 122\) nm
Common mistake: 91 nm (B) uses 13.6 eV, the series limit. 365 nm (C) uses 3.4 eV.
Key point: This ultraviolet line is the first line of the Lyman series.

questions.sub_topic: emf of a cell from two load readings
questions.question: A cell sends a current of 0.5 A through a \(2\ \Omega\) resistor and 0.25 A through a \(5\ \Omega\) resistor. The emf of the cell is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1.5 V
Given: \(I_1 = 0.5\) A with \(R_1 = 2\ \Omega\); \(I_2 = 0.25\) A with \(R_2 = 5\ \Omega\)
Formula: \(\varepsilon = I(R + r)\)
Step 1: \(0.5(2 + r) = 0.25(5 + r) \Rightarrow 1 + 0.5r = 1.25 + 0.25r \Rightarrow r = 1\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(\varepsilon = 0.5(2 + 1) = 1.5\) V
Common mistake: 1 V (A) or 1.25 V (D) is the terminal voltage in one case (\(IR\)), ignoring the internal resistance.
Key point: Two readings give two equations for the two unknowns \(\varepsilon\) and \(r\).

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Fields and forces of currents — which claims fail
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The field inside a long solenoid is nearly uniform.
(B) The field at the centre of a circular loop is proportional to the current in it.
(C) The magnetic force on a moving charge does no work on it.
(D) Two parallel wires carrying currents in opposite directions attract each other.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: currents in opposite directions repel; currents in the same direction attract.
Why not the others: (A) \(B = \mu_0nI\) does not depend on position well inside. (B) \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}\). (C) the force is always perpendicular to the velocity. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Like currents attract, which is the opposite of like charges.

questions.sub_topic: Field on the axis of a small dipole at 10 cm
questions.question: Charges of \(+10\) nC and \(-10\) nC are 2 mm apart. The electric field at a point 10 cm from the centre of this dipole, on its axis, is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 360 N C⁻¹
Given: \(q = 10^{-8}\) C, \(2a = 2 \times 10^{-3}\) m, \(r = 0.1\) m (\(r \gg a\))
Formula: \(p = q(2a)\), \(E_{axial} = \dfrac{2kp}{r^3}\)
Step 1: \(p = 10^{-8} \times 2 \times 10^{-3} = 2 \times 10^{-11}\) C m
Step 2: \(E = \dfrac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 10^{-11}}{10^{-3}} = 360\) N C⁻¹
Common mistake: 180 N C⁻¹ (A) uses the equatorial formula \(\dfrac{kp}{r^3}\).
Key point: The axial field of a dipole is twice the equatorial field at the same distance.

questions.sub_topic: Series, parallel and terminal voltage — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Resistors in series all carry the same current.
(B) The equivalent resistance of resistors in parallel is less than the smallest of them.
(C) The terminal voltage of a cell always equals its emf.
(D) Ohm's law does not hold for a semiconductor diode.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A) there is only one path for the charge. (B) each extra branch gives the current another path. (D) a diode's \(V\)–\(I\) graph is not a straight line through the origin.
Why not the others: (C) is false: when the cell supplies current, \(V = \varepsilon - Ir < \varepsilon\); \(V = \varepsilon\) only on open circuit. Options (C) and (D) include (C); (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: Internal resistance takes part of the emf whenever current flows.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Field inside a 500-turn solenoid
questions.question: A solenoid 0.5 m long has 500 turns and carries 2 A. The field inside it is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(2.5 \times 10^{-3}\) T
Given: \(N = 500\), \(l = 0.5\) m, \(I = 2\) A
Formula: \(B = \mu_0nI\), \(n = \dfrac{N}{l}\)
Step 1: \(n = 1000\) m⁻¹
Step 2: \(B = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 1000 \times 2 \approx 2.5 \times 10^{-3}\) T
Common mistake: \(1.26 \times 10^{-3}\) T (A) uses \(N\) in place of \(n\).
Key point: \(n\) is turns per metre, not the total turns.

questions.sub_topic: Image formed by refraction at a convex glass surface
questions.question: A convex spherical surface of radius 20 cm separates air from glass (\(n = 1.5\)). A point object in air is 100 cm from the surface. The image in the glass is formed at a distance from the surface of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 100 cm
Given: \(n_1 = 1\), \(n_2 = 1.5\), \(u = -100\) cm, \(R = +20\) cm
Formula: \(\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1.5}{v} + \dfrac{1}{100} = \dfrac{0.5}{20} = \dfrac{1}{40}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{1.5}{v} = \dfrac{1}{40} - \dfrac{1}{100} = \dfrac{3}{200}\), so \(v = 100\) cm
Common mistake: 43 cm (B) takes \(u = +100\) cm, adding the two terms.
Key point: Keep the sign convention: distances against the incident light are negative.

questions.sub_topic: Potential energy as two like charges approach
questions.question: When two positive point charges are brought closer together, the electrostatic potential energy of the system:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) increases
Why: \(U = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r}\) is positive for like charges and grows as \(r\) falls; work must be done against their repulsion.
Why not the others: (A) would be true for unlike charges. (C) and (D) ignore the \(\dfrac{1}{r}\) dependence.
Key point: Work done against the field is stored as potential energy.

questions.sub_topic: Field from the force on a test charge
questions.question: A charge of \(2\ \mu\text{C}\) placed at a point experiences a force of 0.04 N. The electric field at that point is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(2 \times 10^{4}\) N C⁻¹
Given: \(F = 0.04\) N, \(q = 2 \times 10^{-6}\) C
Formula: \(E = \dfrac{F}{q}\)
Step 1: \(E = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-2}}{2 \times 10^{-6}} = 2 \times 10^4\) N C⁻¹
Common mistake: \(8 \times 10^{-8}\) (A) multiplies \(F\) and \(q\). \(5 \times 10^{-5}\) (D) inverts the ratio.
Key point: Field is force per unit charge.

questions.sub_topic: Formulas for capacitance, energy density and surface fields
questions.question:
Match each quantity in List-I with its expression in List-II.

List-I
(A) Capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor
(B) Energy density of an electric field
(C) Field just outside a charged conductor
(D) Field of an infinite plane sheet of charge

List-II
(I) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0E^2\)
(II) \(\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\)
(III) \(\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\)
(IV) \(\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Step 1: \(C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}\) (IV)
Step 2: \(u = \dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0E^2\) (I)
Step 3: A conductor's field exists on one side only, so Gauss gives \(\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\) (II)
Step 4: A thin sheet sends field to both sides, so \(\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\) (III)
Common mistake: Swapping (C) and (D); the conductor's field is twice the sheet's because there is no field inside the conductor.
Key point: Draw the Gaussian pillbox and count the faces with flux.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Ratio of de Broglie wavelengths of a proton and an α-particle
questions.question: A proton and an α-particle are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference. The ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths \(\dfrac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(2\sqrt{2}\)
Given: \(m_\alpha = 4m_p\), \(q_\alpha = 2q_p\)
Formula: \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_\alpha q_\alpha}{m_pq_p}}\)
Step 2: \(= \sqrt{4 \times 2} = 2\sqrt{2}\)
Common mistake: 2 (A) uses the mass ratio alone and forgets the double charge. \(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\) (D) inverts the ratio.
Key point: The kinetic energy gained is \(qV\), so charge matters as well as mass.

questions.sub_topic: Power of two identical bulbs joined in series
questions.question: Two identical bulbs, each rated 100 W, 220 V, are joined in series across a 220 V supply. The total power drawn is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 50 W
Given: \(R = \dfrac{220^2}{100} = 484\ \Omega\) each
Formula: \(P = \dfrac{V^2}{R_{total}}\)
Step 1: \(R_{total} = 968\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(P = \dfrac{48400}{968} = 50\) W
Common mistake: 200 W (A) adds the ratings as if each bulb still had 220 V across it. 25 W (D) is the power of one bulb.
Key point: The resistance is fixed by the rating; the power depends on the actual voltage.

questions.sub_topic: Reactance of a 100/π μF capacitor at 50 Hz
questions.question: The reactance of a capacitor of \(\dfrac{100}{\pi}\ \mu\text{F}\) at 50 Hz is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(100\ \Omega\)
Given: \(C = \dfrac{10^{-4}}{\pi}\) F, \(\nu = 50\) Hz
Formula: \(X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\nu C}\)
Step 1: \(2\pi\nu C = 2\pi \times 50 \times \dfrac{10^{-4}}{\pi} = 10^{-2}\)
Step 2: \(X_C = 100\ \Omega\)
Common mistake: \(0.01\ \Omega\) (B) forgets to take the reciprocal.
Key point: A capacitor's reactance falls as the frequency rises.

questions.sub_topic: Intrinsic and doped semiconductors — which claims fail
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) In an intrinsic semiconductor, the number of free electrons equals the number of holes.
(B) At 0 K, pure silicon behaves as an insulator.
(C) Doping silicon with boron makes it an n-type semiconductor.
(D) The conductivity of a semiconductor increases with temperature.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: boron is trivalent, an acceptor, so it makes silicon p-type.
Why not the others: (A) each electron freed leaves one hole. (B) at 0 K no electron has energy to cross the gap. (D) heating frees more carriers. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Group 13 dopant → p-type; group 15 dopant → n-type.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Force on an electron crossing a field
questions.question: An electron moves at \(2 \times 10^6\) m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.1 T. The force on it is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(3.2 \times 10^{-14}\) N
Given: \(q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C, \(v = 2 \times 10^6\) m s⁻¹, \(B = 0.1\) T
Formula: \(F = qvB\)
Step 1: \(F = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2 \times 10^6 \times 0.1 = 3.2 \times 10^{-14}\) N
Common mistake: \(3.2 \times 10^{-20}\) (B) leaves out the speed's power of ten.
Key point: The force is perpendicular to both \(v\) and \(B\).

questions.sub_topic: Wavelength ranges of four bands
questions.question:
Match each band in List-I with its wavelength range in List-II.

List-I
(A) Radio waves
(B) Microwaves
(C) Visible light
(D) X-rays

List-II
(I) 400 nm to 700 nm
(II) longer than 0.1 m
(III) 0.1 m to 1 mm
(IV) 1 nm to \(10^{-3}\) nm
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)
Step 1: Radio: \(> 0.1\) m (II)
Step 2: Microwaves: 0.1 m to 1 mm (III)
Step 3: Visible: 400 to 700 nm (I)
Step 4: X-rays: 1 nm to \(10^{-3}\) nm (IV)
Common mistake: Swapping (A) and (B); microwaves are shorter than radio waves.
Key point: The NCERT table lists bands from long to short wavelength.

questions.sub_topic: Microscopic expressions in current electricity
questions.question:
Match each quantity in List-I with its expression in List-II (\(\tau\) = relaxation time, \(n\) = electron density).

List-I
(A) Current density
(B) Drift velocity
(C) Resistivity
(D) Mobility

List-II
(I) \(\dfrac{eE\tau}{m}\)
(II) \(\dfrac{e\tau}{m}\)
(III) \(\sigma E\)
(IV) \(\dfrac{m}{ne^2\tau}\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Step 1: Ohm's law in vector form: \(J = \sigma E\) (III)
Step 2: \(v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}\) (I)
Step 3: \(\rho = \dfrac{m}{ne^2\tau}\) (IV)
Step 4: \(\mu = \dfrac{v_d}{E} = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}\) (II)
Common mistake: Swapping (B) and (D); mobility is drift velocity per unit field, so it has no \(E\).
Key point: A longer relaxation time means faster drift and lower resistivity.

questions.sub_topic: Phase between current and voltage in a.c. circuits
questions.question:
Match each a.c. circuit in List-I with its phase relation in List-II.

List-I
(A) Pure resistor
(B) Pure inductor
(C) Pure capacitor
(D) Series LCR circuit with \(X_L > X_C\)

List-II
(I) Current in phase with voltage
(II) Current lags voltage by an angle between 0 and \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
(III) Current lags voltage by \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
(IV) Current leads voltage by \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Step 1: Resistor: \(V\) and \(I\) peak together (I)
Step 2: Inductor: current lags by \(90^\circ\) (III)
Step 3: Capacitor: current leads by \(90^\circ\) (IV)
Step 4: \(X_L > X_C\): the circuit is inductive, \(\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}\), so the lag is less than \(90^\circ\) (II)
Common mistake: Swapping (B) and (C); remember "ELI the ICE man": in L, emf before current; in C, current before emf.
Key point: Resistance keeps the phase angle of an LCR circuit below \(90^\circ\).

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Maximum kinetic energy for light of frequency 10¹⁵ Hz
questions.question: Light of frequency \(1 \times 10^{15}\) Hz falls on a metal of work function 2.5 eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is about (\(h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\) J s):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1.6 eV
Given: \(\nu = 10^{15}\) Hz, \(\phi_0 = 2.5\) eV
Formula: \(K_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0\)
Step 1: \(h\nu = 6.6 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 4.1\) eV
Step 2: \(K_{max} = 4.1 - 2.5 = 1.6\) eV
Common mistake: 4.1 eV (A) is the photon energy, before subtracting the work function. 6.6 eV (B) forgets to convert joules to eV.
Key point: Convert J to eV by dividing by \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\).

questions.sub_topic: General features of EM waves — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Electromagnetic waves carry energy and momentum.
(B) The speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum is \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}\).
(C) Infrared waves are often called heat waves.
(D) Microwaves have a shorter wavelength than X-rays.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) EM waves exert radiation pressure. (B) Maxwell found \(c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}\). (C) infrared readily excites molecular vibrations, heating matter.
Why not the others: (D) is false: microwaves (about 1 mm to 0.1 m) are far longer than X-rays (below 1 nm). Options (B) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} = 3 \times 10^8\) m s⁻¹.

questions.sub_topic: Main use of a p–n junction diode
questions.question: A p–n junction diode is mainly used as a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) rectifier
Why: A diode conducts easily only when forward biased, so it lets current through in one direction, turning a.c. into pulsating d.c.
Why not the others: Amplifiers and oscillators need active devices, not a single diode. A diode is not used as a capacitor in ordinary circuits.
Key point: One-way conduction is the diode's defining property.

questions.sub_topic: Self-inductance of a long solenoid
questions.question: A solenoid 0.5 m long has 1000 turns and a cross-section of 10 cm². Its self-inductance is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2.5 mH
Given: \(N = 1000\), \(l = 0.5\) m, \(A = 10^{-3}\) m²
Formula: \(L = \dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{l}\)
Step 1: \(\mu_0N^2A = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 10^6 \times 10^{-3} = 4\pi \times 10^{-4}\)
Step 2: \(L = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-4}}{0.5} = 8\pi \times 10^{-4} \approx 2.5 \times 10^{-3}\) H
Common mistake: 2.5 μH (C) takes 10 cm² as \(10^{-6}\) m². 1.26 mH (A) forgets to divide by the length \(l = 0.5\) m.
Key point: \(L\) grows as \(N^2\).

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Net field at the centre of concentric coils with opposite currents
questions.question: Two concentric circular loops lie in the same plane. The inner one (radius 10 cm) carries 5 A clockwise and the outer one (radius 20 cm) carries 4 A anticlockwise. The field at the common centre is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(6\pi \times 10^{-6}\) T
Given: \(R_1 = 0.1\) m, \(I_1 = 5\) A; \(R_2 = 0.2\) m, \(I_2 = 4\) A; opposite senses
Formula: \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}\)
Step 1: \(B_1 = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 5}{0.2} = 10\pi \times 10^{-6}\) T
Step 2: \(B_2 = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 4}{0.4} = 4\pi \times 10^{-6}\) T
Step 3: Opposite directions: \(B = 10\pi - 4\pi = 6\pi \times 10^{-6}\) T
Common mistake: \(14\pi \times 10^{-6}\) T (A) adds the fields, ignoring the opposite currents.
Key point: Opposite currents give opposite fields at the centre.

questions.sub_topic: Ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier on 60 Hz
questions.question: A full-wave rectifier is fed from a 60 Hz a.c. supply. The fundamental frequency of its output ripple is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 120 Hz
Given: input frequency 60 Hz
Formula: full-wave: two output pulses per input cycle
Step 1: Output frequency \(= 2 \times 60 = 120\) Hz
Common mistake: 60 Hz (A) is the output of a half-wave rectifier.
Key point: Full-wave rectification uses both halves of each cycle.

questions.sub_topic: Nuclear force and binding energy — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) At nuclear distances, the nuclear force is much stronger than the Coulomb force.
(B) The nuclear force between two neutrons is attractive.
(C) The binding energy per nucleon is greatest for nuclei with mass number around 56.
(D) The mass of a nucleus is greater than the sum of the masses of its free nucleons.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) it overcomes proton repulsion. (B) the nuclear force is nearly the same for n–n, p–p and n–p. (C) the binding energy curve peaks near iron (about 8.75 MeV).
Why not the others: (D) is false: the nucleus is lighter than its free nucleons; the difference is the mass defect. Options (C) and (D) include (D); (B) leaves out (C).
Key point: Mass defect × \(c^2\) = binding energy.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Work function from a threshold wavelength
questions.question: The threshold wavelength of a metal is 310 nm. Its work function is about (\(hc = 1240\) eV nm):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4 eV
Given: \(\lambda_0 = 310\) nm
Formula: \(\phi_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0}\)
Step 1: \(\phi_0 = \dfrac{1240}{310} = 4\) eV
Common mistake: 0.25 eV (D) inverts the ratio.
Key point: A longer threshold wavelength means a smaller work function.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Torque on a bar magnet at 30° to a field
questions.question: A bar magnet of magnetic moment 2 A m² makes an angle of \(30^\circ\) with a uniform field of 0.3 T. The torque on it is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.3 N m
Given: \(m = 2\) A m², \(B = 0.3\) T, \(\theta = 30^\circ\)
Formula: \(\tau = mB\sin\theta\)
Step 1: \(mB = 0.6\)
Step 2: \(\tau = 0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.3\) N m
Common mistake: 0.52 N m (B) uses \(\cos 30^\circ\). 0.6 N m (C) is the maximum torque.
Key point: A bar magnet behaves like a current loop in a field.

questions.sub_topic: Capacitance with a dielectric slab filling half the gap
questions.question: A parallel plate air capacitor has capacitance 6 pF. A dielectric slab of \(K = 2\) and thickness equal to half the plate separation is placed between the plates. The new capacitance is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 8 pF
Given: \(C_0 = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d} = 6\) pF, \(t = \dfrac{d}{2}\), \(K = 2\)
Formula: \(C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d - t + \frac{t}{K}}\)
Step 1: \(d - \dfrac{d}{2} + \dfrac{d}{4} = \dfrac{3d}{4}\)
Step 2: \(C = \dfrac{4}{3}C_0 = 8\) pF
Common mistake: 12 pF (B) treats the gap as completely filled. 9 pF (C) averages 6 and 12 pF.
Key point: A partial slab acts like two capacitors in series.

questions.sub_topic: Deviation by a thin prism
questions.question: A thin prism of angle \(6^\circ\) is made of glass of refractive index 1.5. The deviation it produces is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(3^\circ\)
Given: \(A = 6^\circ\), \(n = 1.5\)
Formula: \(\delta = (n - 1)A\)
Step 1: \(\delta = 0.5 \times 6^\circ = 3^\circ\)
Common mistake: \(9^\circ\) (A) uses \(nA\).
Key point: A thin prism's deviation does not depend on the angle of incidence.

questions.sub_topic: Nuclei in increasing order of radius
questions.question:
Arrange these nuclei in increasing order of radius:
(A) \(^{16}\text{O}\)
(B) \(^{4}\text{He}\)
(C) \(^{208}\text{Pb}\)
(D) \(^{56}\text{Fe}\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (A), (D), (C)
Step 1: \(R = R_0A^{1/3}\), so radius increases with mass number
Step 2: \(A\): 4 (He), 16 (O), 56 (Fe), 208 (Pb)
Step 3: Increasing: (B), (A), (D), (C)
Common mistake: (D) reverses the order.
Key point: Radius grows only as the cube root of \(A\): lead is about 3.7 times as wide as helium, not 52 times.

questions.sub_topic: Image of an object inside the focus of a concave mirror
questions.question: A shaving mirror is concave with a focal length of 15 cm. A face held 10 cm from it sees an image located:
options: A) 6 cm in front of the mirror, real and inverted
B) 30 cm in front of the mirror, real and inverted
C) 6 cm behind the mirror, virtual and erect
D) 30 cm behind the mirror, virtual, erect, three times the size
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 30 cm behind the mirror, virtual, erect, three times the size
Given: \(u = -10\) cm, \(f = -15\) cm
Formula: \(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{1}{30}\), so \(v = +30\) cm (behind)
Step 2: \(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = +3\): virtual, erect, magnified
Common mistake: (C) adds \(\dfrac{1}{15}\) and \(\dfrac{1}{10}\), giving 6 cm.
Key point: An object inside \(F\) of a concave mirror gives a magnified virtual image, as in a shaving mirror.

questions.sub_topic: Refractive index from the speed of light in glass
questions.question: Light travels at \(2 \times 10^8\) m s⁻¹ in a glass. The refractive index of the glass is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1.5
Given: \(c = 3 \times 10^8\) m s⁻¹, \(v = 2 \times 10^8\) m s⁻¹
Formula: \(n = \dfrac{c}{v}\)
Step 1: \(n = \dfrac{3}{2} = 1.5\)
Common mistake: 0.67 (B) inverts the ratio, giving \(n < 1\).
Key point: Light is slower in every material medium, so \(n > 1\).

questions.sub_topic: Flux through a closed surface around two charges
questions.question: A closed surface encloses charges of \(3\ \mu\text{C}\) and \(-1\ \mu\text{C}\). The net electric flux through it is about (\(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\) C² N⁻¹ m⁻²):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(2.26 \times 10^{5}\) N m² C⁻¹
Given: \(q_{enc} = 3 - 1 = 2\ \mu\text{C}\)
Formula: \(\Phi = \dfrac{q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}\)
Step 1: \(\Phi = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-6}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 2.26 \times 10^5\) N m² C⁻¹
Common mistake: \(4.5 \times 10^5\) (A) adds the sizes of the charges, \(4\ \mu\text{C}\).
Key point: Only the net enclosed charge matters; the shape of the surface does not.

questions.sub_topic: emf induced by mutual inductance
questions.question: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 0.5 H. The current in the first coil rises steadily from 0 to 2 A in 0.1 s. The emf induced in the second coil is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 10 V
Given: \(M = 0.5\) H, \(\Delta I = 2\) A, \(\Delta t = 0.1\) s
Formula: \(\varepsilon = M\dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = 20\) A s⁻¹
Step 2: \(\varepsilon = 0.5 \times 20 = 10\) V
Common mistake: 1 V (A) multiplies \(M\) by \(\Delta I\) and forgets to divide by \(\Delta t\).
Key point: The emf depends on how fast the current changes, not on its size.

questions.sub_topic: Potential at the centre of a square of four charges
questions.question: Charges of \(2\) nC, \(-1\) nC, \(3\) nC and \(-2\) nC are placed at the corners of a square of side \(\sqrt{2}\) m. The potential at the centre of the square is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 18 V
Given: distance of each corner from the centre \(= \dfrac{\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2}}{2} = 1\) m
Formula: \(V = k\sum\dfrac{q_i}{r}\)
Step 1: \(\sum q_i = (2 - 1 + 3 - 2)\) nC \(= 2\) nC
Step 2: \(V = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 10^{-9}}{1} = 18\) V
Common mistake: 72 V (B) adds the sizes of the charges and ignores their signs. 12.7 V (C) uses the side, not the half-diagonal, as the distance.
Key point: Potential is a scalar: add the charges with their signs.

questions.sub_topic: Voltage across the inductor at resonance
questions.question: A series LCR circuit has \(R = 20\ \Omega\) and \(X_L = X_C = 100\ \Omega\) at the supply frequency. It is connected to 220 V (rms). The rms voltage across the inductor is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1100 V
Given: resonance, so \(Z = R = 20\ \Omega\)
Formula: \(I = \dfrac{V}{R}\), \(V_L = IX_L\)
Step 1: \(I = \dfrac{220}{20} = 11\) A
Step 2: \(V_L = 11 \times 100 = 1100\) V
Common mistake: 220 V (A) assumes no part can exceed the supply voltage; \(V_L\) and \(V_C\) cancel each other, so each can be far larger.
Key point: At resonance the voltages across L and C are equal and opposite.

questions.sub_topic: Energy released by a mass defect of 0.02 u
questions.question: In a nuclear reaction the total mass decreases by 0.02 u. The energy released is about (1 u = 931.5 MeV):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 18.6 MeV
Given: \(\Delta m = 0.02\) u
Formula: \(E = \Delta m \times 931.5\) MeV
Step 1: \(E = 0.02 \times 931.5 \approx 18.6\) MeV
Common mistake: 1.86 MeV (A) or 186 MeV (D) misplaces the decimal.
Key point: 1 u of mass is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

questions.sub_topic: Wavelength from a measured fringe width
questions.question: In Young's experiment, the slits are 0.5 mm apart and the screen is 1.5 m away. The fringe width is 1.2 mm. The wavelength of the light is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 400 nm
Given: \(d = 5 \times 10^{-4}\) m, \(D = 1.5\) m, \(\beta = 1.2 \times 10^{-3}\) m
Formula: \(\lambda = \dfrac{\beta d}{D}\)
Step 1: \(\beta d = 6 \times 10^{-7}\)
Step 2: \(\lambda = \dfrac{6 \times 10^{-7}}{1.5} = 4 \times 10^{-7}\) m \(= 400\) nm
Common mistake: 600 nm (A) forgets to divide by \(D\).
Key point: Fringe width is proportional to wavelength.

questions.sub_topic: Bands in increasing order of frequency
questions.question:
Arrange these in increasing order of frequency:
(A) infrared
(B) X-rays
(C) microwaves
(D) ultraviolet
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (C), (A), (D), (B)
Step 1: Frequency increases as wavelength decreases
Step 2: Wavelength: microwaves > infrared > ultraviolet > X-rays
Step 3: Increasing frequency: (C), (A), (D), (B)
Common mistake: (B) lists the bands in increasing wavelength instead.
Key point: \(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}\).

questions.sub_topic: Lenses, microscope and telescope — which claims fail
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) A ray through the optical centre of a thin lens passes undeviated.
(B) The magnifying power of a simple microscope decreases when its focal length is made smaller.
(C) The power of a concave lens is negative.
(D) In normal adjustment, a telescope forms the final image at infinity.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: \(m = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f}\), so a shorter focal length gives a larger magnifying power.
Why not the others: (A) the centre acts like a thin parallel slab. (C) \(f < 0\) for a diverging lens, so \(P = \dfrac{1}{f} < 0\). (D) parallel rays leave the eyepiece. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Short-focus lenses magnify more.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Field 5 cm from a wire carrying 10 A
questions.question: A long straight wire carries 10 A. The magnetic field 5 cm from it is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(4 \times 10^{-5}\) T
Given: \(I = 10\) A, \(r = 0.05\) m
Formula: \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi} = 2 \times 10^{-7}\)
Step 2: \(B = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 10}{0.05} = 4 \times 10^{-5}\) T
Common mistake: \(1.26 \times 10^{-4}\) T (D) uses the loop formula \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2r}\).
Key point: The field of a long wire falls as \(\dfrac{1}{r}\).

questions.sub_topic: Peak current from an rms reading
questions.question: An a.c. ammeter reads 5 A. The peak value of the current is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 7.07 A
Given: \(I_{rms} = 5\) A
Formula: \(I_0 = \sqrt{2}I_{rms}\)
Step 1: \(I_0 = 1.414 \times 5 \approx 7.07\) A
Common mistake: 3.54 A (A) divides by \(\sqrt{2}\) instead of multiplying.
Key point: a.c. meters read rms values.

questions.sub_topic: Focal length of a glass lens immersed in water
questions.question: A glass lens (\(n = 1.5\)) has a focal length of 20 cm in air. Its focal length when immersed in water (\(n = \dfrac{4}{3}\)) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 80 cm
Given: \(n_g = 1.5\), \(n_w = \dfrac{4}{3}\), \(f_{air} = 20\) cm
Formula: \(\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\dfrac{n_g}{n_m} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)\)
Step 1: In air: \(n_g - 1 = 0.5\); in water: \(\dfrac{1.5}{4/3} - 1 = 0.125\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{f_w}{f_{air}} = \dfrac{0.5}{0.125} = 4\), so \(f_w = 80\) cm
Common mistake: 26.7 cm (B) multiplies by \(\dfrac{4}{3}\), as if the focal length scaled with the index of water.
Key point: In a medium closer to its own index, a lens bends light less.

questions.sub_topic: Magnifying power of a simple microscope at the near point
questions.question: A convex lens of focal length 5 cm is used as a simple microscope with the image at the near point (25 cm). Its magnifying power is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 6
Given: \(f = 5\) cm, \(D = 25\) cm
Formula: \(m = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{D}{f} = 5\)
Step 2: \(m = 6\)
Common mistake: 5 (A) uses \(\dfrac{D}{f}\), which applies when the image is at infinity.
Key point: Image at the near point gives one more than \(\dfrac{D}{f}\).
